stories.headline: Update: Iran Seizes Two Ships in Strait of Hormuz as U.S. Declares Blockade
stories.summary:
Iran has seized two cargo ships in the Strait of Hormuz, including the Epaminondas, as the conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran intensifies. President Trump declared that the U.S. is blockading the Strait of Hormuz and warned that American forces will respond to any Iranian attack on ships in the waterway. Iran has struck targets in Bahrain and Jordan in addition to the maritime confrontations, while Iranian officials assert that Tehran will determine the right of passage through the strategically critical shipping route.

The escalation is sending shockwaves through global energy markets, with oil prices returning to around $100 a barrel and fuel costs rising across Europe. An Iranian military group has also warned the United Kingdom over allowing U.S. forces to use British bases for strikes on Iran, and the Houthi movement has claimed hits on additional vessels while maintaining its maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia.

The broadening of hostilities to the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly 20% of the world's oil supply passes — marks a significant new phase in a conflict that began February 28. Iran's options are widely viewed as limited, with no clear path to victory, while the human cost continues to mount; a strike in the opening hours of the war killed 120 children in Minab, with grief still raw nearly five months later.

The conflict has cost the U.S. at least $37.5 billion to date, according to Defense Secretary Hegseth, who faced a disrupted congressional hearing this week as lawmakers pressed for details. The House passed a war powers resolution to halt the operation in a bipartisan rebuke, though the White House has resisted constraints on executive authority over the campaign.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Expands Wildberries Drone Campaign, Hitting Multiple Russian Logistics Hubs
stories.summary:
Ukrainian drones have struck multiple warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, in a sustained campaign spanning several days. New attacks overnight into Wednesday targeted Wildberries logistics hubs in Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region, following earlier strikes at Elektrostal east of Moscow, Kotovsk in the Tambov region, and Koledino south of Moscow. Company owner Tatiana Kim confirmed additional casualties from the latest strikes.

Kyiv said the facilities are used to supply sanctioned components for drone production and navigation equipment, framing the campaign as a legitimate military target. President Volodymyr Zelensky declared that Ukraine is "quite justly bringing the war back home — to Russia." Russia's Kremlin has denied that online retail platforms serve military supply purposes.

The attacks have dealt a severe blow to hundreds of small and medium-sized Russian businesses that rely on the platform, with one seller posting a viral social media complaint about losing 1 million roubles (approximately $12,700) overnight. Wildberries and its rival Ozon are estimated to serve 85–90% of Russia's economically active population, and in remote regions many Russians depend on them for basic goods.

The campaign represents a strategic evolution in Ukraine's long-range drone warfare, which had previously concentrated on oil depots, refineries, and energy infrastructure. Russia has similarly targeted Ukrainian logistics infrastructure, including warehouses of postal operator Nova Poshta and retail chain ATB, underscoring how both sides are increasingly weaponizing economic disruption.

stories.headline: South Africa's Ramaphosa Wins Temporary Court Halt to Impeachment Inquiry Over 'Farmgate' Scandal
stories.summary:
A South African court has ruled in favor of President Cyril Ramaphosa's bid to temporarily block a parliamentary impeachment inquiry tied to the so-called "Farmgate" scandal. Western Cape High Court Judge Andre le Grange, in a two-to-one majority ruling, halted the parliamentary committee from proceeding until a separate court reviews Ramaphosa's challenge to the inquiry panel's findings. That review case is scheduled to be heard in September.

The impeachment process was revived after the Constitutional Court ruled in May that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the inquiry panel's 2022 report, which found Ramaphosa may have a case to answer. The scandal stems from a 2020 robbery at his private Phala Phala farm in Limpopo, during which thieves allegedly stole $580,000 in U.S. dollar bills hidden in a sofa — money Ramaphosa says came from the sale of buffalo. Critics, including former spy chief Arthur Fraser, accused him of concealing the theft from police and tax authorities and potentially violating foreign exchange laws.

Ramaphosa's legal team argued that allowing the impeachment proceedings to continue while his separate legal challenge was pending would cause irreparable reputational harm. The president welcomed Friday's ruling, saying he "respects" the court's decision. His ANC party no longer commands a parliamentary majority, governing instead through a coalition formed after the 2024 election, which has complicated his political standing.

The ruling effectively delays what had promised to be a significant constitutional test for South Africa's governance. Opposition parties and civil society groups have argued the impeachment process should proceed unimpeded, while Ramaphosa's supporters contend the original panel misinterpreted both its mandate and the evidence before it.

stories.headline: Update: Turkish Opposition Leader Ozel and 90 Lawmakers Quit CHP to Form New Party
stories.summary:
Turkish opposition leader Ozgur Ozel and 90 other lawmakers resigned from the Republican People's Party (CHP) on Friday to establish a new political party aimed at unifying a fractured opposition against President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. The exodus represents one of the largest splits in the CHP's history and follows months of internal divisions over strategy and leadership direction within Turkey's main opposition force.

The defections leave the CHP significantly weakened in parliament and raise questions about whether a splintered opposition can mount an effective challenge to Erdogan's ruling AKP ahead of future elections. Ozel and his allies argue that a new vehicle is needed to mobilize disillusioned voters who have grown frustrated with the CHP's internal conflicts and electoral failures.

The development comes as Turkey's political landscape remains turbulent. A previously covered story noted that a deposed Turkish opposition leader had already announced plans to challenge Erdogan through new political structures, and Friday's mass resignation represents a concrete crystallization of that broader opposition realignment. Turkey's government has yet to formally respond to the formation of the new grouping.

The fracturing of the CHP could paradoxically help Erdogan by dividing the vote share of opposition parties, or could — if the new party generates momentum — consolidate anti-government sentiment under fresh leadership. Political analysts in Ankara said the outcome will depend heavily on whether Ozel's new movement can attract significant public support beyond the parliamentary faction that followed him out of the CHP.
